title: Loops and arrays
goal: Repeat work over servers, files and lines safely with for, while and until, and keep lists in arrays.
setup: # P1: inventory file with comments, an empty line, and an END marker
# P5: broken loop script, with a Windows path in the input

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Print the line count of every .log file in logs/,' '# then print each path in paths.txt exactly as written, and count them.' 'COUNT=0' 'for f in $(ls logs/*.log); do' '  echo "$f: $(wc -l < "$f") lines"' 'done' 'cat paths.txt | while read p; do' '  echo "path: [$p]"' '  COUNT=$((COUNT + 1))' 'done' 'echo "paths read: $COUNT"' > count-loop.sh
printf '%s\n' 'web-01 OK' 'web-02 SKIP' 'web-03 OK' 'db-01 FAIL' 'db-02 OK' > results.txt

warmup.q: What is the difference between `[ ]` and `[[ ]]` with an empty variable?
warmup.a: `[ $x = a ]` fails with `unary operator expected`. `[[ $x = a ]]` works, because `[[ ]]` does not split variables.

warmup.q: Which test checks that a file exists and is not empty?

warmup.a: Spaces around `=`. Bash runs `APP` as a command: `APP: command not found`. Write `APP=todo`.

warmup.q: Which exit code means "command not found"?

problems.title: Read an inventory file line by line
problems.situation: An Ansible-style inventory `inventory.csv` lists servers as `host,port,env`. It has comment lines (`#`), an empty line, and an `END` marker; lines after `END` are retired servers. The user must print one line per real server.
task: Read the file with `while IFS=, read -r host port env; do ... done < inventory.csv`.
Skip empty lines and lines that start with `#` (use `continue`).
Stop the loop at the line `END` (use `break`).
Print `HOST:PORT (ENV)` for each server, and a count at the end.
hints: `IFS=,` splits each line at commas. `-r` keeps backslashes as they are.
Skip test: `[[ -z $host || $host == \#* ]] && continue`.
Stop test: `[[ $host == END ]] && break`. Use `< inventory.csv` after `done`, not `cat |`.
solution: while IFS=, read -r host port env; do

explanation.part: while IFS=, read -r a b c
explanation.meaning: Read one line each time. `IFS=,` = split at commas, only for this `read`.
Raw: a backslash `\` stays a backslash. Always use `-r`.
Skip the rest of this loop round and read the next line.
Leave the loop completely.
A pattern for "starts with #". The `\` stops `#` from starting a comment.
The loop reads from the file. The loop stays in the main shell, so `COUNT` keeps its value.

mistakes: Using `for line in $(cat inventory.csv)`: it splits at every space and new line, not per line.
`cat inventory.csv | while read ...`: the loop runs in a subshell, so `COUNT` is 0 after the loop (see P5).
Forgetting the last line: if the file has no new line at the end, `read` fails on it. Use `while IFS=, read -r a b c || [[ -n $a ]]`.
problems.interview_say: To read a file line by line I use `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`. `-r` keeps backslashes, `IFS` controls splitting, and redirecting the file keeps variables in the main shell.
problems.try_yourself: Change the loop to collect only `prod` servers into one line: `web-01 web-02`.

problems.title: Four kinds of for loops
problems.situation: The user needs loops for daily tasks: run a command on three web servers, retry a step 3 times, and count lines in every log file, even when a file name has a space.
task: List loop: `for host in web-01 web-02 db-01; do echo "ssh $host uptime"; done` (dry run).
Brace range: loop over `web-{01..03}`.
C-style loop: `for ((i = 1; i <= 3; i++))` and print `attempt $i of 3`.
File loop: `for f in logs/*.log` and print the name and line count. Quote `"$f"`.
hints: `{01..03}` keeps the leading zero: 01 02 03.
In `(( ))` no `$` is needed: `((i++))`.
Let bash expand the wildcard: `for f in logs/*.log`, never `$(ls logs/*.log)`.
solution: for host in web-01 web-02 db-01; do
echo "ssh $host uptime"            # dry run: print the command
for host in web-{01..03}; do echo "check $host"; done
for ((i = 1; i <= 3; i++)); do echo "attempt $i of 3"; done

explanation.part: for x in a b c
explanation.meaning: Run once for each word in the list.
Brace range: web-01 web-02 web-03.
C-style loop with a counter: start; condition; step.
Bash expands the wildcard into file names. Names with spaces stay one item.
Quote the loop variable, or `worker 2.log` breaks into two words.

problems.expected_output:
ssh web-01 uptime
ssh web-02 uptime
ssh db-01 uptime
check web-01
check web-02
check web-03
attempt 1 of 3
attempt 2 of 3
attempt 3 of 3
logs/api.log: 2 lines
logs/web.log: 3 lines
logs/worker 2.log: 1 lines
mistakes: `for i in {1..$N}` does not work: braces expand before variables. Use `for ((i = 1; i <= N; i++))` or `seq 1 "$N"`.
No match: if `logs/*.log` matches nothing, the loop runs once with the text `logs/*.log`. Check with `[ -e "$f" ] || continue`.

checks.run: N=3; for i in {1..$N}; do echo $i; done

problems.interview_say: I use a list loop for hosts, a C-style loop for counters and retries, and a glob like `for f in *.log` for files, always quoting `"$f"` because names can have spaces.
problems.try_yourself: Run `N=3; for i in {1..$N}; do echo $i; done`. What prints? Why?

problems.title: until: wait for the database to be ready
problems.situation: In `docker compose`, the backend often starts before the database is ready and then crashes. A start script must wait until the database answers, but not forever: at most 5 tries.
task: Use the given fake check `db_ready` (it succeeds on the 3rd call).
Write an `until db_ready; do ... done` loop that prints `waiting for db (try N)`.
Stop with an error message and `exit 1` after 5 tries.
After the loop, print `db is ready after N tries`.
hints: `until CMD` loops while CMD fails. It is the opposite of `while CMD`.
Count with `TRY=$((TRY + 1))` and test `[ "$TRY" -ge 5 ]` inside the loop.
In real life use `sleep 2` between tries. Here `sleep 0.2` keeps it fast.
solution: db_ready() { CALLS=$((CALLS + 1)); [ "$CALLS" -ge 3 ]; }   # fake: ready on the 3rd call
if [ "$TRY" -ge 5 ]; then echo "db not ready after $TRY tries" >&2; exit 1; fi

explanation.meaning: Repeat the body while `cmd` fails (exit code not 0).
A fake check. A real one could be `pg_isready -h db` or `nc -z db 5432`.
Never wait forever in automation. Fail clearly after a limit.
Wait between tries so the loop does not use 100% CPU.

problems.expected_output:
waiting for db (try 1)
waiting for db (try 2)
db is ready after 3 tries
mistakes: No limit: an `until` loop without a counter can run forever and block the pipeline.
No `sleep`: the loop checks thousands of times per second and floods the logs.
problems.interview_say: I use `until check; do sleep 2; done` to wait for a dependency, always with a maximum number of tries and a clear error, so a pipeline never hangs forever.
problems.try_yourself: Change the fake check to succeed on the 7th call. What does the script print, and what is the exit code?

problems.title: Indexed and associative arrays
problems.situation: A release script must build three Docker images (a list), and must know the port of each service (a name-to-number map). Bash has indexed arrays for lists and associative arrays for maps.
task: Create `IMAGES=(todo-frontend todo-backend "todo worker")`. Print the count, the first item, and all items one per line.
Add `todo-cron` to the end with `+=`. Print the count again.
Create a map: `declare -A PORTS=([frontend]=80 [backend]=8080 [db]=5432)`.
Print the port of `backend`. Then loop over all keys (sorted) and print `key -> port`.
Check if the key `cache` exists.
hints: `${#ARR[@]}` = count, `${ARR[0]}` = first item, `"${ARR[@]}"` = all items, each one separate.
Associative arrays need `declare -A`. `${!MAP[@]}` gives the keys.
Keys have no fixed order. Sort them: `printf '%s\n' "${!PORTS[@]}" | sort`.
solution: for img in "${IMAGES[@]}"; do echo "build: $img"; done
[[ -v PORTS[cache] ]] && echo "cache is set" || echo "no port for cache"

explanation.meaning: Indexed array with 3 items. Quotes keep `c d` as one item.
Number of items / first item (index 0) / last item.
All items, each one as a separate word. Always quote it.
Add an item at the end.
Associative array: keys are names, not numbers.
All keys. The order is random, so sort them for stable output.
True if the key exists.

problems.expected_output:
count: 3, first: todo-frontend
build: todo-frontend
build: todo-backend
build: todo worker
count now: 4, last: todo-cron
backend port: 8080
backend -> 8080
db -> 5432
frontend -> 80
no port for cache
mistakes: `for img in ${IMAGES[@]}` without quotes splits `todo worker` into two images.
Forgetting `declare -A`: bash makes an indexed array, every key becomes 0, and only the last value stays.
Using `$IMAGES` alone: it gives only the first item.

checks.run: IMAGES=(a b "todo worker"); for i in ${IMAGES[@]}; do echo "[$i]"; done

problems.interview_say: I use indexed arrays for lists, like images to build, and `declare -A` maps for name-to-value data, like service ports. I always loop with `"${arr[@]}"` in quotes.
problems.try_yourself: Run `unset 'IMAGES[1]'` and print `${!IMAGES[@]}` (the indexes). Is index 1 gone? Is the count 3?

problems.title: Find the bug: the counting loop
problems.situation: `count-loop.sh` should print the line count of every log, then each path from `paths.txt` exactly as written (one is a Windows path), and the number of paths. The output is wrong in three places.
task: Run `bash count-loop.sh` and compare with the goal in the comments.
Find 3 bugs: the file loop, the `read` options, and the pipe into `while`.
Fix them and run again. The Windows path must keep its backslashes `\`, and the third path must keep its 2 leading spaces.
hints: `$(ls logs/*.log)` splits `worker 2.log` at the space.
Without `-r`, `read` eats backslashes. Without `IFS=`, it removes leading spaces.
`cat file | while ...` runs the loop in a subshell; COUNT is lost. Use `done < paths.txt`.
solution: # Print the line count of every .log file in logs/,
# then print each path in paths.txt exactly as written, and count them.
for f in logs/*.log; do                  # let bash expand the glob
while IFS= read -r p; do                 # IFS= keeps spaces, -r keeps backslashes
done < paths.txt                         # no pipe: COUNT survives

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: `$(ls ...)` gave words, not names. `worker 2.log` became `logs/worker` and `2.log`.
Bug 2: `-r` keeps `\`. `IFS=` (empty) keeps leading and trailing spaces.
Bug 3: with `cat ... |`, the loop was a subshell, so `COUNT` was back to 0 after it.

problems.expected_output:
logs/api.log: 2 lines
logs/web.log: 3 lines
count-loop.sh: line 6: logs/worker: No such file or directory
logs/worker:  lines
count-loop.sh: line 6: 2.log: No such file or directory
2.log:  lines
path: [C:Userswickytodo-app]
path: [/var/log/todo]
path: [/opt/todo/config]
paths read: 0
--- fixed ---
logs/api.log: 2 lines
logs/web.log: 3 lines
logs/worker 2.log: 1 lines
path: [C:\Users\wicky\todo-app]
path: [/var/log/todo]
path: [  /opt/todo/config]
paths read: 3
mistakes: Thinking `C:Userswickytodo-app` is a typo in the file. It is `read` without `-r` removing the backslashes.
Moving `echo "paths read"` inside the loop to "fix" the count. The real fix is to remove the pipe.
problems.interview_say: The safe pattern is `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`. Looping over `$(ls)` breaks on spaces, and piping into `while` loses variables because of the subshell.
problems.try_yourself: Keep the pipe but add `shopt -s lastpipe` at the top of the script. Does COUNT work now? (It works in scripts, not in an interactive shell.)

problems.title: Stop at the first failure: break and continue
problems.situation: A rolling deploy updates servers one by one. Servers marked `SKIP` are in maintenance. If one server returns `FAIL`, the deploy must stop at once so the other servers keep the old, working version.
task: Read `results.txt` (`host status`) line by line.
`SKIP`: print `skip HOST` and `continue`.
`FAIL`: print `FAIL on HOST, stopping rollout`, and `break`.
`OK`: print `updated HOST`. After the loop, print how many servers were updated.
hints: Use `case "$status" in ... esac` inside the loop.
`continue` jumps to the next line; `break` leaves the loop.
`db-02` must not be updated, because `db-01` failed before it.
solution: FAIL) echo "FAIL on $host, stopping rollout"; break ;;

explanation.meaning: Go to the next loop round (next server).
Leave the loop. Lines after `db-01` are never read.
A common pattern: read a status, then decide.

problems.expected_output:
updated web-01
skip web-02
updated web-03
FAIL on db-01, stopping rollout
servers updated: 2
mistakes: Using `exit` instead of `break`: the whole script ends and the summary line is never printed.
Using `break` in a nested loop and expecting both loops to end. Use `break 2` for two levels.
problems.interview_say: In a rolling update I loop over servers, `continue` for ones in maintenance, and `break` on the first failure so the rest keep the working version.
problems.try_yourself: Change `break` to `break 2` and wrap the `while` loop in `for round in 1 2; do ... done`. What changes?

problems.title: Loop over command output: mapfile and < <( )
problems.situation: The user wants to loop over the output of a command (for example a list of pods or files) and still keep counters after the loop. Two safe ways: `mapfile` into an array, or a loop that reads from `< <(command)`.
task: Read the log file names into an array: `mapfile -t FILES < <(printf '%s\n' logs/*.log)`.
Print how many files there are, and each one in brackets.
Count lines over all files with `while IFS= read -r f; do ... done < <(printf '%s\n' logs/*.log)`.
Print the total after the loop.
hints: `<(command)` is process substitution: bash gives the command output as a file.
`mapfile -t ARR` reads lines into an array; `-t` removes the new line at the end of each line.
The loop reads from `< <(...)`, so it runs in the main shell and `TOTAL` keeps its value.
solution: for f in "${FILES[@]}"; do echo "[$f]"; done

explanation.meaning: Process substitution: the output of `cmd` looks like a file.
Redirect that "file" into the loop. Note the space between `<` and `<(`.
Read every line into the array ARR (also called `readarray`).

mistakes: Writing `<<(cmd)` without the space: `syntax error near unexpected token` (bash reads it as a here-doc).
Using `mapfile` in `sh`: it is a bash feature. Run the script with `bash`.

checks.run: printf 'while read x; do echo $x; done <<(echo hi)\n' > t.sh; bash t.sh

problems.interview_say: To loop over command output without losing variables, I use `while IFS= read -r x; do ...; done < <(cmd)` or `mapfile -t arr < <(cmd)`.
problems.try_yourself: Use `mapfile -t LINES < inventory.csv` and print `${LINES[1]}`. Which line is it?

interview.q: How do you read a file line by line in bash?
interview.a: `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`. `-r` keeps backslashes, `IFS=` keeps spaces, and the redirect keeps variables in the main shell.

interview.q: Why is `for f in $(ls)` a bad idea?
interview.a: The output is split at spaces, so names with spaces break. Use a glob: `for f in *`.

interview.q: What is the difference between `break` and `continue`?
interview.a: `continue` skips to the next loop round. `break` leaves the loop completely.

interview.q: How do you wait for a service in a script without hanging forever?
interview.a: An `until` (or `while`) loop with a check, a `sleep`, and a maximum number of tries that ends with `exit 1`.

interview.q: What is an associative array, and how do you create one?
interview.a: A map from names to values. `declare -A PORTS=([web]=80)`, then `${PORTS[web]}`. Keys: `${!PORTS[@]}`.
